Learning outcomes
  1. Apply the order of mathematical operations correctly.
  2. Use R as a calculator to evaluate mathematical expressions.
``` ## Order of mathematical operations {#sec-1} - Mathematical operations in an expression are evaluated in a specific order. - Parentheses (and other grouping symbols such as fraction bars and radical bars) are evaluated first, then exponents (and roots), then multiplication and division (left to right), and finally addition and subtraction (left to right). - This sequence is often remembered using the acronym **PEMDAS** (@fig-order-operations). ![Order of mathematical operations](/images/operations-flow1.jpg){#fig-order-operations fig-align="center" width="900"} ::: callout-note ## Operations with the same precedence - When operations have the same precedence (e.g., multiplication and division or addition and subtraction) appear in the same expression, they are evaluated according to the order they appear from left to right. ::: ```{=html}
Worked Examples & Practice
``` ::::: panel-tabset ## Example M.1.1 {{< iconify ic:round-menu-book size=21px >}} Calculate: $\displaystyle \boldsymbol{2\times(3+4)-6 \times 4^2}$ 1. Parentheses (calculate what is inside the parentheses): $(3 + 4) = 7$, so the expression becomes $\xRightarrow\ 2 \times 7-6 \times 4^2$. 2. Exponents: $4^2=16$, so the expression becomes $\xRightarrow\ 2 \times 7-6 \times 16$. 3. Multiplication (left to right): $2 \times 7 = 14$ and $6 \times 16 = 96$, so the expression becomes $\xRightarrow\ 14-96$. 4. Subtraction: $14-96= \boxed{-82}$. ## [Exercise M.1.1 {{< iconify fluent:chat-bubbles-question-20-filled size=21px >}}]{style="color: #ba181b"} ::: {#tabset-M11} Calculate: $\displaystyle \boldsymbol{\left( 3+\frac{4}{2} \right)^3-\sqrt{4\times9}\times2+2}$ :::
1. Parentheses and grouping symbols (calculate what is inside them first following PEMDAS order): $(3 + \displaystyle \frac{4}{2})^3 =(3 + 2)^3 = 5^3$ and $\sqrt{4\times9} = \sqrt{36}$, so the expression becomes $\xRightarrow\ 5^3-\sqrt{36} \times2+2$. 2. Exponents and square roots: $5^3=125$ and $\sqrt{36}=6$, so the expression becomes $\Rightarrow\ 125-6 \times2+2$. 3. Multiplication: $6 \times 2=12$, so the expression becomes $\xRightarrow\ 125-12+2$ 4. Addition and subtraction (from left to right): $125-12=113$ and $113+2= \boxed{115}$.
## [Exercise M.1.2 {{< iconify fluent:chat-bubbles-question-20-filled size=21px >}}]{style="color: #ba181b"} ::: {#tabset-M12} Calculate: $\displaystyle \boldsymbol{\frac{1^2+5^2+7}{4-1}}$ ::: The answer is ::::: ## Using R as calculator {#calculator} - R can be used as a calculator to evaluate different mathematical expressions. - The most common arithmetic operators in R are shown in @tbl-r-operators. | Operation | Operator | |:-----------------------------|:---:| | Addition | $+$ | | Subtraction | $-$ | | Multiplication | $*$ | | Division | $/$ | | Exponentiation | \^ or $**$ | | Integer division (returns the result as integer discarding any remainder) | $\text{\%/\%}$ | | Modulo (returns the remainder of division) | $\text{\%\%}$ | : Table of arithmetic operators in R {#tbl-r-operators tbl-colwidths="[75,25]"}

- Now, let's try to calculate the expression in @tabset-M11 using R and check if it gives the same answer (note that to calculate the square root in R, either raise to the power of $1/2 = 0.5$ or use the `sqrt()` function): ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Option 1: # Rising to the power of 1/2 or 0.5 (3+4/2)^3-(4*9)^0.5*2+2 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 115 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} # Option 2: # Using the sqrt() function (3+4/2)^3-sqrt(4*9)*2+2 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 115 ``` ::: ::: ```{=html}
Worked Examples & Practice
``` ::: panel-tabset ## Example M.1.2 {{< iconify ic:round-menu-book size=21px >}} Use R to perform ordinary division, integer division, and modulo operations using $10$ and $3$. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Ordinary division # Returns the result of the division (3.333333) 10 / 3 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 3.333333 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} # Integer division # Returns the integer quotient (3) discarding the remainder (0.333333) 10 %/% 3 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 3 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} # Modulo # Returns the remainder of the division (1) 10 %% 3 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 1 ``` ::: ::: ## Example M.1.3 {{< iconify ic:round-menu-book size=21px >}} Use R to calculate: $\displaystyle \boldsymbol{4/2 \times 3}$ ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} 4/2*3 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 6 ``` ::: ::: - In this expression, both division and multiplication have the same precedence, but division is performed before multiplication because it appears first from left to right. ## [Exercise M.1.3 {{< iconify fluent:chat-bubbles-question-20-filled size=21px >}}]{style="color: #ba181b"} Use the following interactive R code block to write an R code to calculate the expression we solved before in @tabset-M12. ```{webr-r} # Write your R code here then click "Run Code" to print the answer ``` ::: {.cell webex.hide='Click to show/hide answer'}
```{.r .cell-code} (1^2+5^2+7)/(4-1) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 11 ``` :::
